strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a genuinely broad spectrum of tasks: zero-shot semantic segmentation (Tab. 1), open-vocabulary instance segmentation (Tab. 2), VQA via an LLM pipeline (Tab. 3), linear/decoder probing and full finetuning on five benchmarks (Tab. 4), instance probing (Tab. 6), and data-efficiency studies (Tab. 5), which is more thorough than most prior 3DGS pretraining works.

Consistently strong quantitative results: new state-of-the-art on 4 of 5 fully finetuned semantic segmentation benchmarks (e.g., 79.4 mIoU ScanNet, 52.9 ScanNet++), +6.5 mIoU on ScanNet200, +7.6 mAP on tail classes for open-vocabulary instance segmentation, and clear improvements over SceneSplat across the board.

The render-and-distill adaptation (§3.3) is a practically useful contribution: it eliminates ~1 TB of precomputed teacher features and costly 3D pseudo-label preprocessing (Tab. 7), and the view sampling/pairing pipeline plus the +2.7 mIoU gain from adapting on only 100 scenes (Fig. 6) demonstrate real value for out-of-domain transfer.
The 3DGS-aware augmentations (§3.4) are a thoughtful, problem-specific design grounded in the rendering equation rather than reusing point-cloud augmentations, with ablation support in Fig. 8.

The analysis of why the point-cloud variant transfers (Tab. 8 noise-robustness retrieval experiment, Fig. 6 scaling study, and the staged PE-Spatial finding in Fig. 8) goes beyond reporting numbers and provides testable hypotheses.

Data-efficiency claims (8.32×/39.9× fewer training scenes) are well supported by the limited-scene and limited-annotation experiments, and the teachers ablation (Tab. 9) confirms non-redundant gains from each teacher.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the core recipe is an assembly of existing components — the lift-then-align paradigm and architecture concept come directly from SceneSplat [28], the backbone is adapted from Sonata [55], multi-teacher agglomerative distillation is established in 2D (RADIO, DUNE) and the loss balancing uses PHI-S [41] off-the-shelf. The contribution is primarily a systematic specialization of these ideas to 3DGS rather than a new learning principle.

The data-efficiency comparison to Sonata is arguably not apples-to-apples: Chorus distills from 2D foundation models (SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE) that were pretrained on vastly larger image corpora and from 2D pseudo-labels derived from them, whereas Sonata is purely self-supervised on point clouds. Counting only 'training scenes' understates the total supervision used, so the 39.9× efficiency claim should be more carefully qualified.

Some results are mixed or less favorable but presented with limited discussion: Sonata still leads Chorus on ScanNet instance-segmentation linear probing (72.6 vs 66.6 mAP25, Tab. 6); the VQA METEOR slightly drops (22.5 vs 22.9, Tab. 3); zero-shot Matterport3D with SN-only training trails joint Mosaic3D (Tab. 1). These deserve explicit treatment.

Presentation defects undermine polish and reproducibility in the submitted version: Table 9 contains raw LaTeX ('mIoU_\text{fg}'), Figure 4 appears garbled/broken in the PDF, and reference [26] is a near-duplicate of [25] (both the SAM paper) with seemingly wrong citation keys, suggesting citation management errors.

Key details for reproducibility of the 3DGS-aware augmentations and contrastive terms are deferred to the supplement (equations 'provided in the supplement'), so the main paper alone is insufficient to reimplement these components; the claim of releasing code mitigates this but is unverifiable at review time.

The staged-teacher finding (PE-Spatial only in the second half) and teacher scheduling are presented with limited hyperparameter analysis of the scheduling space, and the total objective involves several free knobs (λt, ηt, staging set A(e)) whose sensitivity is only partially explored.
Pretraining is confined to indoor ScanNet-style scenes from SceneSplat-7K; generalization beyond indoor domains is not tested, limiting evidence for the 'holistic' general-purpose encoder claim.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic and instance segmentation, linear/decoder probing, full finetuning, data-efficiency benchmarks, and LLM-based VQA across five datasets (Tab. 1–6), which is substantially broader than prior 3DGS encoding work such as SceneSplat.

Strong reported results, including state-of-the-art zero-shot semantic segmentation (Tab. 1), large tail-class gains in open-vocabulary instance segmentation (+7.6 mAP on 66 tail classes, Tab. 2), and new finetuned SOTA on 4 of 5 probing benchmarks (Tab. 4).

The render-and-distill adaptation (§3.3, Tab. 7, Fig. 5–6) is a practical contribution: it removes the ~1 TB precomputed-feature storage burden and demonstrates +2.7% mIoU from only 100 adaptation scenes, supported by a concrete resource comparison.

The ablations are reasonably thorough: teacher staging (Fig. 8, Tab. 9), 3DGS-aware augmentations, design choices, runtime (Tab. 10), and a genuinely interesting analysis of why a 3DGS-pretrained encoder transfers to point clouds (Tab. 8, Fig. 6).
The paper is generally well written and organized, with the method grounded explicitly in the rendering equation and uplifting procedure (Eqs. 1–8).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the framework is a fairly direct combination of known components—the lift-then-align paradigm from SceneSplat [28], the Sonata backbone [55], multi-teacher agglomerative distillation in the spirit of RADIO [42,17] with PHI-S balancing [41]. The core recipe is assembling existing pieces rather than introducing a new learning principle.

Teacher-fairness confound: Chorus uses SigLIP2, DINOv3, and PE-Spatial, all substantially newer/stronger 2D models than the single SigLIP teacher in SceneSplat. The paper does not disentangle how much of the reported gain comes from the multi-teacher design itself versus simply upgrading to stronger 2D teachers; a SigLIP-only Chorus vs. SceneSplat comparison is deferred to the supplement and not visible in the main results.

Some headline comparisons are questionable: in the single-dataset (SN) setting of Tab. 1, Chorus actually loses f-mAcc on Matterport3D to SceneSplat (16.4 vs. 18.7), and the '8.32×/39.9× fewer scenes' claims compare against methods trained on different data distributions and objectives (Mosaic3D, Sonata), making the data-efficiency framing partially apples-to-oranges. The point-cloud variant also uses the SceneSplat-7K Gaussian-derived data rather than Sonata's training data, so the Sonata comparison is not controlled.

The 'why does it work on point clouds' analysis (Tab. 8) is thin: 684 instances from only 10 scenes is a small evaluation, and the two-hypothesis explanation is plausible but not rigorously established.

VQA gains are modest and within what could be noise for some metrics (e.g., M on ScanQA drops 22.9→22.5 while R improves, Tab. 3), and the VQA evaluation is a backbone swap inside one specific pipeline (GaussianVLM) rather than a systematic study.

Reproducibility concerns: many critical details (contrastive loss equations, augmentation equations, staged schedule, SigLIP ablation) are deferred to a supplement not provided, and code is only promised 'upon publication'; several implementation choices (loss weights, staging epochs) lack justification.

Presentation issues: duplicated reference entries ([25] vs. [26] both cite SAM), inconsistent metric reporting across tables, and Table 9's mixed 'ScanNet / ScanNet++ v2' training-source formatting make the ablation hard to parse.

strengths: Strong and broad empirical evidence: Chorus is evaluated on open-vocabulary semantic and instance segmentation, linear/decoder probing, full finetuning, data-efficiency regimes, and VQA, across ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and a newly introduced 3DGS-native benchmark (InteriorGS), which is considerably wider than the evaluation scope of prior 3DGS pretraining work such as SceneSplat.

Consistently improved results over the closest prior work: e.g., +3.2 f-mIoU / +9.0 f-mAcc over SceneSplat on ScanNet200 zero-shot, +5.6 f-mIoU on InteriorGS, and notably better probing results versus Sonata (ScanNet200 linear probing 36.0 vs. 28.8 mIoU), with full-finetuning state-of-the-art on 4 of 5 benchmarks.

The point-cloud variant result is an interesting and well-investigated finding: the paper does not merely report that the PC variant competes with Sonata using ~39.9× fewer training scenes, but develops testable hypotheses (noise-robustness via PC→perturbed-PC retrieval in Tab. 8; data-efficiency scaling in Fig. 6) — a level of analysis beyond average result reporting.

The render-and-distill adaptation is practically useful: it removes ~1 TB of precomputed pseudo-label storage (Tab. 7) and demonstrably improves domain adaptation (+2.7 mIoU with only 100 scenes), supported by a resolution/scene-count ablation (Fig. 5).

Reasonable ablations: teacher ablation (Tab. 9) shows non-redundant gains from each teacher, design-choice ablation (Fig. 8) covers loss terms, augmentations, staging, and contrastive terms, and runtime/parameter counts are reported (Tab. 10).
3DGS-aware augmentations (rendering-equivalent and immature-manifold perturbations) are a thoughtful, modality-motivated design rather than blindly reused point-cloud augmentations.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: multi-teacher distillation with per-teacher projectors is established in 2D (RADIO, DUNE), and the overall framework is a fairly direct generalization of SceneSplat's lift-then-align paradigm from one teacher to three. The main novelty lies in the application to 3DGS, the PC variant findings, and the adaptation recipe rather than a fundamentally new method.

Potential fair-comparison ambiguity in Tab. 4: rows labeled '✾/• Chorus' do not clarify which variant (full 3DGS vs. point-cloud-only) achieves the reported number. If the best of two variants is implicitly selected per cell while baselines get a single model, this raises a cherry-picking concern that should be clarified.

Some headline comparisons conflate different training-data conditions: the '8.32×/39.9× fewer scenes' claims compare against Mosaic3D trained on 24.3× more data sources, so the efficiency claim, while valid, should be read carefully as a data-source advantage rather than a pure method advantage in all cases.

VQA gains (Tab. 3) are comparatively modest and the M metric on ScanQA slightly drops (22.5 vs. 22.9), so the 'holistic' claim is somewhat weaker on reasoning tasks; only the last encoder stage is fed to the VLM, leaving the utility of intermediate stages unexamined.

Open-vocabulary instance segmentation depends on externally supplied Mask3D proposals (as do the baselines), so the result measures reranking/probing of frozen proposals rather than end-to-end instance discovery.

Several details are deferred to the supplement, including contrastive loss equations, augmentation equations, SigLIP-teacher ablation, and view-pairing specifics; the main text alone is not fully self-contained for reproduction.

Presentation roughness: minor inconsistencies (text states '0.7s per scene' where ablation context says runtime of 0.7s is practical while Fig. 8 shows different absolute numbers), an acknowledged remaining limitation of expensive offline pseudo-label precomputation for the standard recipe, and some typos/formatting artifacts in equations and figure captions.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across a wide spectrum of tasks and datasets (open-vocabulary semantic/instance segmentation, linear/decoder probing, full finetuning, data-efficiency, LLM-based QA), spanning 3DGS-native (InteriorGS) and point-cloud benchmarks, which substantiates the 'holistic encoder' claim better than a single-benchmark study.

Consistent state-of-the-art or competitive results with clear margins: e.g., +2.1% f-mIoU over SceneSplat on ScanNet200 zero-shot segmentation, +6.5 mIoU over Sonata when finetuned on ScanNet200, +7.6 mAP on tail classes for open-vocabulary instance segmentation, and consistent gains in the low-data regime (Tab. 5).

Data-efficiency claims are supported by controlled comparisons: 8.32×/39.9× fewer training scenes than competing pretraining baselines, and a scaling analysis (Fig. 6) showing faster scaling than self-supervised Sonata on the same 3DGS data.

The render-and-distill adaptation is a practical contribution with a concrete cost analysis (Tab. 7: 8 GB vs ~1 TB storage, <0.1 s/view rasterization) and demonstrated gains (+2.7% mIoU with only 100 adaptation scenes, Fig. 5/6).

The analysis section goes beyond headline numbers: ablations of each teacher (Tabs. 9, C), 3DGS-aware augmentations (Fig. 8), robustness to 3DGS re-optimization and Gaussian density (Tab. 10), iPhone-captured point clouds (Tab. 11), and two testable hypotheses (with a retrieval experiment, Tab. 8) for why the point-cloud variant transfers well.

The supplementary is thorough (detailed pseudo-label processing, augmentations grounded in the rendering equation with a Taylor-expansion argument, pose sampling pipeline, full metric definitions), supporting reproducibility; codebase is stated to be released.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the core recipe assembles existing components — the lift-then-align paradigm and contrastive terms come from SceneSplat, the backbone from Sonata, teacher feature standardization from PHI-S (RADIO), and multi-teacher aggregation is established in 2D (AM-RADIO, DUNE). The contribution is largely a well-executed 3DGS-specific instantiation rather than a new learning principle.

A potential circularity concern in the evaluation: the supervision teachers (SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE-Spatial) are massive web-scale foundation models, so several zero-shot/feature-quality gains may partly reflect distilling a larger-capacity prior rather than better 3D encoding per se. The paper acknowledges representational convergence but does not fully isolate this; comparing against baselines using the same teacher budget would strengthen the claims.

The data-efficiency headline (8.32× vs Mosaic3D, 39.9× vs Sonata) compares against methods trained with different data recipes and modalities; the apples-to-apples comparison is complicated by the re-processed Matterport3D 3DGS data and newly processed pseudo-labels, and the paper re-trains SceneSplat itself to be fair — which is good — but the cross-method efficiency claims still rest on partly different setups.

On the point-cloud benchmarks, the Chorus variant uses the same Sonata backbone architecture, so the gains cannot be attributed to the 3DGS representation itself; the authors address this honestly, but the '3DGS pretraining as strong augmentation' hypothesis remains a partial explanation (retrieval R@1 85.4% vs 79.8% is suggestive but limited to 684 instances from 10 scenes).

Some probing results are mixed: Sonata beats Chorus on ScanNet instance segmentation linear probing (72.6 vs 66.6 mAP25) and on ScanNet decoder probing for semantics; Chorus is also the slowest model at inference (0.70 s/scene). These caveats are reported but under-discussed relative to the SOTA framing.

VQA gains are modest and the setup swaps only the backbone within GaussianVLM, with the Chorus encoder restricted to the final stage; the improvement (e.g., 14.8 vs 14.4 EM1 on ScanQA) is small and may be within run-to-run variance for LLM finetuning pipelines.

The offline teacher pseudo-label preprocessing cost remains a real limitation (acknowledged), and the render-and-distill adaptation is only demonstrated on one out-of-domain dataset (InteriorGS), limiting evidence for generalization of the adaptation recipe.

Minor presentation issues: several equations in the main text appear with unrendered LaTeX labels (e.g., Eq. 1, 2), and some claims of 'first' holistic 3DGS encoder ignore closely related concurrent work (e.g., Gausstr, UniPre3D, Concerto) that the related-work section cites but does not position against quantitatively.

strengths: Broad and convincing empirical evaluation: the paper covers zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (Tab. 1) and instance segmentation (Tab. 2), linear/decoder probing and full finetuning across five benchmarks (Tab. 4), data-efficiency studies (Tab. 5), instance segmentation probing (Tab. 6), and LLM-based QA (Tab. 3), consistently improving over the closest prior works (SceneSplat, Sonata, Mosaic3D).

The multi-teacher design is well-motivated and well-ablated: teacher ablations (Tab. 9, Tab. C) show non-redundant gains from SigLIP2, DINOv3, and PE-Spatial, and the design-choice ablation (Fig. 8) validates SmoothL1, 3DGS-aware augmentations, staged PE introduction, and the contrastive terms individually.

The finding that a 3DGS-pretrained encoder (inputting only centers, colors, normals) transfers to point-cloud benchmarks and matches Sonata with ~39.9x fewer training scenes is genuinely interesting and supported by targeted analysis (Tab. 8 retrieval robustness, Fig. 6 scaling trends, UMAP analysis in Fig. G).

The render-and-distill adaptation is a practical contribution: Tab. 7 shows a large storage reduction (~1TB -> 8GB) and Fig. 5/6 quantify adaptation gains with resolution and scene count, addressing a real bottleneck in the lift-then-align paradigm.

The supplementary material is thorough (contrastive loss derivation, augmentation theory via Taylor expansion of the rendering equation, dataset construction details for InteriorGS), supporting reproducibility; codebase is released.

Robustness checks (MCMC vs standard 3DGS, Gaussian density, iPhone RGB-D captures in Tabs. 10-11) strengthen the claim that the encoder learns generalizable representations rather than exploiting optimization artifacts.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core recipe (lift 2D foundation features as pseudo-labels, train a feed-forward 3D encoder) is directly inherited from SceneSplat, and the multi-teacher aggregation with PHI-S standardization (Eq. 5-6) closely follows established multi-teacher distillation practice (RADIO/PHI-S, DuNe). The paper is best viewed as a careful engineering extension rather than a new paradigm; the 'for the first time in 3DGS' framing overstates this.

The surprising point-cloud transfer result is explained only plausibly, not conclusively: the '3DGS-as-augmentation' hypothesis is tested with a small retrieval experiment on 684 instances from 10 scenes (Tab. 8), which is thin evidence for a headline claim; alternative explanations (e.g., simply much larger effective feature supervision per Gaussian) are not ruled out.

Some comparisons raise fairness questions: the data-efficiency headline (8.32x/39.9x fewer scenes) compares against Mosaic3D trained on a much larger multi-dataset corpus, but Chorus also uses joint SN+SN+++MP3D data in the joint setting; several rows in Tab. 1 report SceneSplat results retrained by the authors rather than taken from the original paper; evaluation on the self-introduced InteriorGS benchmark favors methods distilled from the same teacher families.

A few numbers are internally inconsistent or under-explained: e.g., in Tab. 1 Chorus degrades on Matterport3D f-mAcc vs SceneSplat (16.4 vs 18.7) in the SN-only setting without discussion; decoder probing is sometimes worse than linear probing (Tab. 4 ScanNet/ScanNet200), which is left unanalyzed; the VQA gains (Tab. 3) show Chorus slightly worse on METEOR (22.5 vs 22.9), again unaddressed.

Method description leans heavily on the supplement: the total loss, staging schedule, and augmentation equations are relegated to the supplement, and key hyperparameter sensitivity (η_t, β range for the immature-manifold perturbation) is not characterized in the main text.

Dependence on very recent, large 2D teachers (SigLIP2-so400m, DINOv3-ViT-L, PE-Spatial-L14) makes it hard to attribute gains to the 3D pretraining framework versus simply stronger teachers; an ablation isolating teacher-model quality on a fixed 3D recipe would strengthen the claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: learning general-purpose, transferable features directly from 3DGS primitives, rather than only attaching semantics post-hoc (e.g., LERF, LangSplat-style feature splatting).

The multi-teacher design (SigLIP2 for language alignment, DINOv3 for generalist features, PE-Spatial for object-aware locality) with a shared backbone and lightweight per-teacher projectors is a sensible and clearly motivated instantiation of multi-teacher distillation for 3D, supported by teacher ablations (Tab. 9, Tab. C) showing non-redundant gains from each teacher.

Evaluation breadth is unusually strong: zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (Tab. 1), open-vocabulary instance segmentation (Tab. 2), linear/decoder probing and full finetuning on five benchmarks (Tab. 4), data-efficiency studies (Tab. 5), instance probing (Tab. 6), LLM-based QA (Tab. 3), and robustness analyses (MCMC variants, density, iPhone captures — Tabs. 10, 11).

State-of-the-art or near-SOTA results are reported across tasks, with meaningful margins on finetuned point-cloud benchmarks (e.g., +6.5 mIoU on ScanNet200) and strong open-vocabulary tail-class gains (+7.6 mAP).

The render-and-distill adaptation (Sec. 3.3, Alg. 1) is a practical contribution: it removes the ~1 TB offline pseudo-label storage bottleneck (Tab. 7) and yields measurable adaptation gains (Fig. 6, Fig. 5), including a well-documented view sampling/pairing pipeline.

The ablation on why the point-cloud variant works (Tab. 8 retrieval robustness, Fig. 6 scaling, UMAP analysis in the supplement) is a thoughtful analysis rather than an afterthought; the two 3DGS-aware augmentations are grounded in the rendering equation with a Taylor-expansion argument for rendering preservation.
The supplementary material is thorough (data processing, loss equations, evaluation metrics, additional ablations), and the codebase is stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the core recipe is a combination of established components — the 'lift-then-align' paradigm from SceneSplat, the Sonata backbone, multi-teacher agglomerative distillation (RADIO/DUNE-style), PHI-S standardization, and LUDVIG uplifting. The novelty lies in the combination and specialization to 3DGS rather than in fundamentally new technique; the paper should be careful not to oversell this.

Some comparisons have fairness caveats: the Chorus variant has 131.3M parameters vs. SceneSplat's 91.7M and Mosaic3D's 39.1M (Tab. 12), so parameter count partly explains gains over some baselines; the re-processed Matterport3D 3DGS data also improves the shared data substrate relative to prior work, which complicates attribution of improvements purely to the pretraining method.

The headline '39.9× fewer training scenes' claim compares against Sonata's self-supervised point-cloud pretraining on different data (3DGS scenes vs. point clouds), so it is not a strictly controlled comparison; the paper's own analysis (Tab. 8, Fig. 6) suggests the advantage stems partly from supervision signal and partly from data augmentation effects, which deserves clearer framing as a confound.

VQA results (Tab. 3) show mixed movement: gains on EM1/ROUGE/Sim but METEOR slightly drops on ScanQA (22.5 vs 22.9), and the setup only swaps the 3D backbone in an existing pipeline (GaussianVLM), so the LLM results are supportive but not independently strong evidence.

The teacher ablation for zero-shot segmentation (Tab. 9) conflates dataset effects (ScanNet vs. ScanNet++ v2 rows) with teacher additions, and the biggest jump (adding PE) appears mainly on InteriorGS, making the 'PE is essential' conclusion somewhat dataset-dependent.

Open-vocabulary evaluation relies on pseudo-labels from the very teachers used in pretraining, so the zero-shot metrics partly measure how well the student matches its teachers' label space rather than fully open-world generalization; a discussion of this circularity would strengthen the claims.

Runtime is the slowest among compared encoders (0.70 s/scene, Tab. 12), which the paper acknowledges but does not deeply analyze; the offline teacher feature precomputation cost for full pretraining also remains a limitation only partially addressed by the adaptation recipe.
